concepts.name: Open interest (OI) and OI change
concepts.what: The number of option (or futures) contracts still open at a strike: every contract has one buyer and one seller, so OI counts positions, not trades. OI rises when new positions open and falls when they close.
concepts.use: Traders read rising OI as fresh conviction and falling OI as positions being closed. Big call-OI additions are read as call writing (a ceiling), big put-OI additions as put writing (a floor).
concepts.measure: Read directly from the chain for each strike and side. R61: near-the-money OI = call + put OI at the 5 strikes nearest the money (log10); OI change = % change of call + put OI at the 11 nearest strikes since the day's first chain minute; 'writer tilt' = put OI % change minus call OI % change over 30 minutes.
concepts.phone: yes: ChainAnalytics.oiData / oiProfile / oiChange from the live chain (Dhan or Zerodha)

concepts.role: context or filter only: may make Solo skip or prefer a candidate, never create a trade or pick its side
concepts.verdict: Failed: no OI check helped an arm (OI_FILTER, 145 results; H26, 2,268 variants). In R61 it added nothing to Solo 2.0 (AUC change under 0.01 on 5,780 design candidates and the final days).
pitfalls: OI is published with a lag (NSE updates it every few minutes), so minute-level OI changes are stale.
You cannot tell from OI alone whether the buyer or the seller opened the position.
Lot-size changes and expiry roll-offs move OI without any view behind it.

evidence.finding: No OI or volume check improved the Liquidity arm in both years; the ORB 'volume surge' kept 3% of trades and never reached t = 2.

concepts.name: OI build-up types
concepts.what: Price change and OI change read together: price up + OI up = long build-up (new buyers); price down + OI up = short build-up (new sellers); price up + OI down = short covering (sellers closing); price down + OI down = long unwinding (buyers closing).
concepts.use: A trend is trusted when it comes with build-up on its side (long build-up for up moves) and doubted when it is only covering or unwinding.
concepts.measure: R61: the index's 30-minute change and the 30-minute change of call + put OI at the 11 strikes nearest the money: +2 long build-up, +1 short covering, -1 long unwinding, -2 short build-up, 0 if either is flat. Classic build-up uses FUTURES OI; the lake has index-futures minutes only from Jul 2026, so R61 uses near-the-money option OI instead.

concepts.name: Put-call ratio (PCR), on OI and on volume
concepts.what: Put OI divided by call OI (or put volume / call volume). Above 1: more puts than calls.
concepts.use: Read both ways: as sentiment (many puts = fear, a contrarian buy) or as writing (many puts written = a floor, bullish). Extremes versus the index's own history matter more than the raw level.
concepts.measure: R61: put / call OI at the 11 strikes nearest the money (A2 already uses this level); its change over 30 minutes; put / call volume summed since 09:15; and the rank of today's OI ratio among the last 5 and 20 sessions at the same minute.
concepts.phone: yes: ChainAnalytics.pcr (OI and volume); the ranks need the phone's own stored history of past sessions

pitfalls: The same number is read bullish by one school and bearish by another.
The ratio depends on which strikes are included and on the expiry; compare like with like.
Near expiry, OI shifts fast and the ratio swings without meaning.

concepts.name: Max pain
concepts.what: The expiry price at which option holders, taken together, would get the least money: the strike that minimises the total payout on all open calls and puts.
concepts.use: Folklore says the index is 'pulled' toward max pain into expiry because option writers defend it.
concepts.measure: For each chain strike X: sum over strikes K of call OI x max(X - K, 0) + put OI x max(K - X, 0); max pain = the X with the smallest total (ties: the lowest strike). R61: (max pain - index) / index x 100, signed by the trade's side, over the 21 strikes around the money.

pitfalls: It changes every minute as OI changes, and depends on the strike window used.
It assumes writers can move the index; our data says they do not.

concepts.name: OI walls (support and resistance from OI)
concepts.what: The strike with the most call OI above the index (read as resistance) and with the most put OI below it (read as support).
concepts.use: Option buyers avoid buying calls just under a big call wall; breakouts 'through a wall' are chased.
concepts.measure: R61: % distance from the index to the biggest call-OI strike at or above it and to the biggest put-OI strike at or below it (ties: the nearer one), within the 21 strikes around the money; expressed as 'wall ahead' (on the trade's way) and 'wall behind'.

Far walls just mean the market expects a wide range.

concepts.name: Implied volatility (IV), ATM IV
concepts.what: The volatility that makes the Black-Scholes price equal the option's market price: how much movement the market is paying for. Higher IV = dearer options.
concepts.use: Option buyers prefer cheap IV (less to lose if IV falls) and fear 'IV crush' after events; sellers like high IV.
concepts.measure: From the chain's IV column (the lake and the broker both give it per strike); ATM IV = mean of the at-the-money call and put IV. R61 adds its change since the day's first chain minute.
concepts.phone: yes: ChainAnalytics.ivSmile (ATM IV), broker IV per strike

concepts.role: size/context only: our research says it predicts how much the index may move, not which way
concepts.verdict: Size only: IV says how much the index may move, not which way (VOLATILITY, 249 days). Solo 2.0 already uses ATM IV as one input (128 final trades). In R61 it added nothing to Solo 2.0 (AUC change under 0.01 on 5,780 design candidates and the final days).
pitfalls: A buyer can be right on direction and still lose when IV falls.
IV is quoted per expiry; weekly IV near expiry is noisy.
Bad ticks in thin strikes give absurd IVs (R61 removes them before use).

evidence.finding: Day range rose with opening IV: 464 / 540 / 631 points by IV third (83 days each). Descriptive.
Buying when IV is cheap versus a realised-vol forecast: best -Rs 30 a day net, q 0.80; 0 of 12 filters adopted.

concepts.name: IV rank and IV percentile
concepts.what: Where today's IV sits in its own past: IV rank = (IV - lowest) / (highest - lowest) over a look-back; IV percentile = share of past days with lower IV.
concepts.use: Buy options when IV rank is low, sell when it is high.
concepts.measure: R61: ATM IV rank (min-max) among the previous 60 sessions at the same minute (needs 40 sessions; Boss's Nov 2024 data rule makes 252-day ranks too short to train on).

concepts.name: IV skew and smile
concepts.what: How IV differs across strikes. Skew: out-of-the-money puts usually carry higher IV than calls (crash insurance). Smile: both wings dearer than the middle.
concepts.use: Steep put skew = demand for protection (fear); flattening skew = calm. Some read rising call skew as upside speculation.
concepts.measure: A2: put IV 3 strikes below minus call IV 3 strikes above (skew). R61 adds smile curvature = (put IV -3 + call IV +3) / 2 - ATM IV. 25-delta skew is NOT used: deltas of far strikes on a 21-strike chain are noisy; the +-3-strike version is the stated substitute.

concepts.name: IV term structure
concepts.what: IV of the next expiry versus a later one. Normally later expiries carry slightly higher IV (contango); near-term IV above far-term (backwardation) signals near-term stress or an event.
concepts.use: Backwardation warns of an event or panic; option buyers prefer the expiry whose IV is relatively cheap.
concepts.measure: R61: NIFTY only, monthly-file ATM IV minus weekly-file ATM IV (0 when both are the same contract). For BANKNIFTY, FINNIFTY and MIDCPNIFTY there are only monthly expiries since 20 Nov 2024, so there is no second expiry in the lake to compare (missing).

concepts.name: Delta
concepts.what: How much the option's price moves for a 1-point move in the index (0 to 1 for calls, 0 to -1 for puts); also roughly the chance of expiring in the money.
concepts.use: Pick strikes (ITM = higher delta, behaves like the index), size positions, convert an index view into option points.
concepts.measure: Black-Scholes: call N(d1), put N(d1) - 1, d1 = (ln(S/K) + (r + s^2/2) T) / (s sqrt T), from the contract's own IV; R61 uses r = 6.5% and T = (sessions to expiry + rest of today / 375) / 252.

concepts.name: Gamma
concepts.what: How fast delta changes as the index moves. High gamma (at the money, near expiry) = the option's exposure grows quickly in a move, both ways.
concepts.use: Buyers like gamma for fast moves (expiry-day 'hero' trades); sellers fear it.
concepts.measure: Black-Scholes gamma = pdf(d1) / (S s sqrt T); R61 reports it as the change in delta for a 1% index move (gamma x S x 0.01).

concepts.name: Theta (time decay)
concepts.what: How much value the option loses per day if nothing else changes. Always a cost to the buyer; biggest at the money and near expiry.
concepts.use: Buyers want the move to come before decay eats the premium; time stops exist because of theta.
concepts.measure: Black-Scholes theta per session (1/252 year); R61 reports it as % of the premium.

concepts.name: Gamma exposure (GEX) and the gamma-flip level
concepts.what: An estimate of how much option dealers must buy or sell the index to stay hedged as it moves. If dealers are long gamma (positive GEX) they sell rallies and buy dips (calmer market); short gamma (negative GEX) they chase moves (wilder market). The flip is the index level where net GEX changes sign.
concepts.use: Positive GEX: fade moves, expect ranges. Negative GEX / below the flip: expect trends and bigger moves.
concepts.measure: Net GEX = sum over strikes of (call gamma x call OI - put gamma x put OI) x S^2 x 0.01, assuming dealers are long calls and short puts (the convention R28 used). R61: net / gross (between -1 and +1), its sign, and the % distance to the level (within +-3%) where net GEX, re-priced, changes sign.
concepts.phone: yes: ChainAnalytics.gex / gammaDensity (note: the phone prices from the forward; a port must match R61's definition exactly)
concepts.sourceText: Option chain: context or filter only, never the signal by default.

concepts.name: Order flow: delta and cumulative delta (CVD)
concepts.what: Delta = volume traded at the ask (aggressive buyers) minus volume at the bid (aggressive sellers) in a bar; cumulative delta adds it up through the day. Divergence (price up, CVD down) is read as weak buying.
concepts.use: Confirm a breakout with positive delta; fade a move whose delta diverges.
concepts.measure: Needs every trade with its side (tick rule or bid / ask). The lake has only 1-minute bars, so R61b uses a proxy: each index minute's close location ((C - L) - (H - C)) / (H - L) weighted by that minute's near-ATM option volume, over 30 minutes (`delta30`) and from 09:15 (`cdelta_day`), signed by the trade's side. TickZoneRecorder computes the real tick-rule delta and CVD per minute from 12 Oct 2026.

concepts.name: Order-flow imbalance (OFI)
concepts.what: The net change in the best bid and ask queues between quotes: bids growing or asks being taken pushes OFI up. Academic work finds it explains same-time price changes very well.
concepts.use: HFT and scalpers lean on short-horizon OFI; discretionary traders watch the bid / ask stack.
concepts.measure: Needs every best-bid / best-ask update (Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov 2014). Not computable from minute bars. R61b's nearest proxy: the near-ATM call minus put volume share over 15 minutes (`optvol_imb15`), signed by side; it is an activity tilt, not OFI.

concepts.name: Zigzag (swing highs and lows)
concepts.what: A line joining the chart's alternating swing highs and swing lows, ignoring the smaller wiggles in between. It turns a price chart into a list of 'the last high, the last low, the high before it, the low before it'.
concepts.use: To see the trend at a glance (higher highs and higher lows = up) and to place stops beyond the last swing.
concepts.measure: EmreKb's script (length 9): the trend turns down when a bar's low is the lowest of the last 9 bars and up when a bar's high is the highest of the last 9; the extreme since the last turn becomes the swing. A swing is only known 9 bars later.

concepts.role: context only: a way to describe the recent swings; never a trade rule on its own
concepts.verdict: Context only; as R62b's swing source no variant passed (0 of 16, 5 indices).
pitfalls: A swing is only known AFTER price has moved away from it; a zigzag drawn back at the swing bar looks perfect in hindsight (repainting).
The length decides everything: a short one finds many small swings, a long one few late ones.
On an intraday chart the zigzag runs across the overnight gap.

concepts.name: Market structure break (MSB)
concepts.what: The moment the chart's swing pattern turns: in a downtrend, price makes a high that clears the last swing high by a clear margin (bullish MSB); the mirror for an uptrend (bearish MSB).
concepts.use: As the signal that the trend has changed side, and as the trigger that creates an order block to trade on the pullback.
concepts.measure: EmreKb compares confirmed zigzag swings, not a close: bullish when the newest swing high is above the previous one by more than fib x the last leg; bearish the mirror. After a break, a new swing high and low are needed before the next one.

concepts.name: Fib breakout confirmation (fib factor)
concepts.what: A margin a break must clear before it counts: a new swing must go beyond the old one by a fraction (the fib factor) of the last swing leg, so small pokes beyond a level are ignored.
concepts.use: A larger factor means fewer, 'cleaner' breaks; a smaller one more, earlier breaks.
concepts.measure: Bullish break needs the new high above the old by more than fib x the leg; bearish the mirror. The script's default is 0.33, the video uses 0.273; R62b also tried 0.50.
